GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus:
The General GI Wall Plan ⭐

Every part of the gut tube from oesophagus to anus has the same four layers — learn them once and apply them everywhere:

🔬 Image slot — oesophageal wall showing the four layers
LayerContents
MucosaEpithelium + lamina propria + muscularis mucosae
SubmucosaConnective tissue, vessels, Meissner's (submucosal) plexus; sometimes glands
Muscularis externaInner circular + outer longitudinal smooth muscle; Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus between them
Serosa / adventitiaMesothelium (serosa) or connective tissue (adventitia)
Oesophagus — Specifics
  • Epithelium: non-keratinised stratified squamous — resists abrasion from food
  • Submucosal mucous glands (lubrication)
  • Muscularis externa: skeletal muscle (upper 1/3) → mixed (middle) → smooth muscle (lower 1/3)
  • Mostly adventitia (retroperitoneal-like); only the short abdominal part has a serosa
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Barrett's oesophagus
Reflux → squamous → columnar (intestinal) metaplasia → risk of adenocarcinoma.
Squamous cell carcinoma
Upper/mid oesophagus; smoking & alcohol.
Achalasia / varices
Myenteric-plexus loss (achalasia); submucosal venous varices in portal hypertension.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • GI wall (everywhere): mucosa → submucosa (Meissner) → muscularis externa (Auerbach) → serosa/adventitia.
  • Oesophagus = non-keratinised stratified squamous + submucosal glands.
  • Muscle: skeletal (upper) → smooth (lower); mostly adventitia.
  • Barrett's = squamous→columnar metaplasia (adenocarcinoma risk).
GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (layers, gland:
Overview

The stomach mixes and digests food. Its mucosa is simple columnar epithelium dipping into gastric pits that lead to gastric glands; it also has an extra oblique muscle layer for churning.

🔬 Image slot — gastric (fundic) mucosa showing pits, glands, parietal and chief cells
Gastric Gland Cell Types ⭐
CellSecretesLook/location
Surface/mucous neck cellsProtective mucus + bicarbonateLine pits & gland necks
Parietal (oxyntic) cellsHCl + intrinsic factorEosinophilic (pink), 'fried-egg'; upper gland
Chief (zymogenic) cellsPepsinogen (+ gastric lipase)Basophilic (blue); gland base
Enteroendocrine cellse.g. G cells → gastrin (antrum); ECL → histamineScattered
Regions: cardia/pylorus = mostly mucous glands; fundus/body = the acid-secreting glands (parietal + chief cells).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Peptic ulcer / gastritis
H. pylori (Giemsa-stained), NSAIDs → mucosal damage.
Pernicious anaemia
Autoimmune loss of parietal cells → intrinsic factor deficiency → B12 malabsorption.
Intestinal metaplasia → cancer
Chronic gastritis → metaplasia/dysplasia → adenocarcinoma (incl. signet-ring 'linitis plastica').
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Parietal cells (pink, upper gland) → HCl + intrinsic factor; chief cells (blue, base) → pepsinogen.
  • G cells (antrum) → gastrin; ECL cells → histamine.
  • Surface mucus + bicarbonate protect the mucosa; extra oblique muscle layer for churning.
  • Pernicious anaemia = parietal-cell loss (no intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency); H. pylori → ulcers.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Small Intestine (villi:
Overview — Built for Absorption

The small intestine maximises absorptive surface area three ways: plicae circulares (folds), villi, and microvilli (brush border) — together ~600× amplification.

🔬 Image slot — small intestine: villi, crypts of Lieberkühn, goblet cells and a lacteal
  • Villi = finger-like mucosal projections; each contains a capillary network + a central lacteal (lymphatic for fat)
  • Crypts of Lieberkühn = glands at the base (stem-cell zone)
  • Epithelium: simple columnar with a brush border (enterocytes) + goblet cells
Specialised Cells & Regional Features
FeatureDetail
EnterocytesAbsorptive cells with a microvillous brush border
Goblet cellsMucus (increase toward the ileum)
Paneth cellsEosinophilic granules at crypt base; secrete antimicrobials (defensins, lysozyme)
Enteroendocrine cellsSecretin, CCK, etc.
DuodenumBrunner's glands (submucosal) → alkaline mucus
IleumPeyer's patches (lymphoid aggregates) + most goblet cells
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Coeliac disease
Villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytes → malabsorption.
Crohn's disease
Transmural inflammation + non-caseating granulomas (often terminal ileum).
Carcinoid tumour
Enteroendocrine-cell tumour → serotonin (carcinoid syndrome).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Surface area: plicae circulares → villi → microvilli (brush border).
  • Each villus has a lacteal (fat absorption); crypts of Lieberkühn hold the stem cells.
  • Paneth cells (crypt base, antimicrobial); Brunner's glands = duodenum; Peyer's patches = ileum.
  • Coeliac = villous atrophy (blunted villi + crypt hyperplasia + IELs).
GASTROINTESTINAL__Large Intestine:
Overview

The colon reabsorbs water and electrolytes and compacts faeces. Its mucosa has straight tubular crypts but NO villi, and is packed with goblet cells for lubrication.

🔬 Image slot — colonic mucosa: straight test-tube crypts, abundant goblet cells, flat surface (no villi)
  • Simple columnar epithelium (colonocytes + abundant goblet cells); no villi; straight 'test-tube' crypts
  • Outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three bands = taeniae coli (form haustra)
  • Appendix: similar but small lumen with abundant lymphoid tissue in the wall
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Ulcerative colitis
Mucosal inflammation, crypt abscesses, continuous from the rectum; dysplasia risk.
Colorectal adenoma → carcinoma
Adenomatous polyps (dysplastic crypts) → adenocarcinoma sequence.
Hirschsprung / diverticula
Absent myenteric ganglia (Hirschsprung); mucosal outpouchings (diverticulosis).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Colon = NO villi, straight tubular crypts, abundant goblet cells; taeniae coli (haustra).
  • Ulcerative colitis = crypt abscesses, continuous mucosal disease from the rectum.
  • Adenoma → carcinoma sequence; appendix is rich in lymphoid tissue.
  • Hirschsprung = absent ganglion cells in the distal colon.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Liver (lobule, sinusoi:
Overview — The Classic Lobule

The liver is organised into hexagonal lobules: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, with portal triads at the corners.

🔬 Image slot — liver lobule: central vein, radiating hepatocyte plates, sinusoids and a portal triad
Central vein
  • Drains blood out (→ hepatic vein → IVC), at the lobule centre
Portal triad (corners)
  • Portal vein branch + hepatic artery branch + bile duct (+ lymphatic)
Sinusoids & Blood Flow
  • Sinusoids = leaky (discontinuous, fenestrated) capillaries between hepatocyte plates; carry mixed portal + arterial blood toward the central vein
  • Lined by endothelium + Kupffer cells (resident macrophages)
  • Space of Disse (between endothelium and hepatocytes) contains hepatic stellate (Ito) cells — store vitamin A; become fibrogenic in cirrhosis
  • Bile canaliculi run between hepatocytes toward the bile duct — bile flows opposite to blood
Zones & the Acinus
Zone 1 (periportal) — best oxygenated; first hit by toxins/viruses
Zone 3 (centrilobular / pericentral) — least oxygenated; most vulnerable to ischaemia & paracetamol/alcohol toxicity
The acinus (blood-flow unit) explains this oxygen gradient
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cirrhosis
Stellate-cell-driven fibrosis + regenerative nodules; distorted architecture.
Centrilobular necrosis
Zone 3 damage in ischaemia/shock and paracetamol overdose.
Viral hepatitis / fatty liver
Hepatocyte injury; steatosis (fat vacuoles) in alcohol/NAFLD.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Lobule: central vein in the middle, portal triads (portal vein + hepatic artery + bile duct) at the corners.
  • Blood flows portal→central; bile flows central→portal (opposite directions).
  • Sinusoids: Kupffer cells (macrophages); space of Disse holds stellate (Ito) cells (vitamin A; fibrosis).
  • Zone 3 (centrilobular) = least oxygenated → ischaemia & paracetamol/alcohol damage.
GASTROINTESTINAL__Gallbladder:
Overview

The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile. Its wall is simple: mucosa, muscle and adventitia/serosa — no submucosa and no muscularis mucosae.

🔬 Image slot — gallbladder wall: tall columnar epithelium with mucosal folds and Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses
  • Tall simple columnar epithelium with microvilli (absorbs water to concentrate bile), thrown into folds when empty
  • No goblet cells normally; no muscularis mucosae, no submucosa
  • A smooth-muscle layer contracts (via CCK) to expel bile; outer adventitia (liver side) / serosa (free side)
  • Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses = epithelial outpouchings into the wall
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Cholelithiasis / cholecystitis
Gallstones → obstruction & inflammation; deepened Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses.
Porcelain gallbladder
Chronic inflammation → wall calcification (cancer risk).
Adenocarcinoma
Uncommon; associated with gallstones/chronic inflammation.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Gallbladder = tall columnar epithelium, mucosal folds; no muscularis mucosae, no submucosa.
  • Concentrates bile by water absorption; contracts to CCK.
  • Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses = mucosal herniations (prominent in chronic cholecystitis).
GASTROINTESTINAL__Pancreas (exocrine & e:
Overview — Two Glands in One Organ

The pancreas is a mixed gland: a large exocrine part (digestive enzymes) with scattered endocrine islets of Langerhans.

🔬 Image slot — pancreas: dark serous acini with a pale islet of Langerhans among them
Exocrine Pancreas
  • Serous acini of pyramidal cells with basophilic bases (RER) and apical zymogen granules (eosinophilic) — secrete digestive proenzymes (trypsinogen, amylase, lipase)
  • Centroacinar cells begin the duct system and secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid
  • Ducts: intercalated → intralobular → interlobular → main pancreatic duct
  • No striated ducts and no myoepithelial cells (unlike salivary glands)
Endocrine Pancreas

The islets of Langerhans (pale clusters) contain β (insulin), α (glucagon), δ (somatostatin) and PP cells — see the dedicated Islets of Langerhans note (Endocrine).

Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Acute pancreatitis
Enzyme autodigestion → fat necrosis + inflammation (gallstones, alcohol).
Chronic pancreatitis
Acinar loss, fibrosis, duct dilatation → malabsorption & diabetes.
Ductal adenocarcinoma
Aggressive; usually in the head; desmoplastic stroma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Pancreas = serous acini (zymogen granules) + islets (endocrine).
  • Centroacinar cells are unique to the pancreas → bicarbonate-rich fluid.
  • No striated ducts / no myoepithelial cells (distinguishes it from salivary glands).
  • Acute pancreatitis = enzyme autodigestion + fat necrosis (gallstones/alcohol).
GASTROINTESTINAL__Salivary Glands:
Overview

The three paired major salivary glands make saliva via serous and mucous acini drained by a characteristic duct system.

🔬 Image slot — salivary gland: serous acini, mucous acini with serous demilunes, and a striated duct
GlandSecretion
ParotidMostly serous (watery, enzyme-rich)
SubmandibularMixed (serous > mucous)
SublingualMostly mucous
Cells, Demilunes & Ducts
  • Serous cells (pyramidal, basophilic, zymogen granules) vs mucous cells (pale, foamy, basal nucleus)
  • Serous demilunes = caps of serous cells over mucous acini
  • Myoepithelial cells hug the acini and squeeze out secretion
  • Duct system: intercalated → striated (basal infoldings + mitochondria → modify electrolytes) → excretory
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Sialolithiasis
Duct stones (commonest in submandibular) → obstruction & swelling on eating.
Pleomorphic adenoma
Commonest salivary tumour (parotid); mixed epithelial + myoepithelial + chondromyxoid stroma.
Sjögren / mumps
Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltrate (Sjögren → dry mouth); viral parotitis (mumps).
⭐ Exam Pearls
  • Parotid = serous; sublingual = mucous; submandibular = mixed.
  • Serous demilunes cap mucous acini; myoepithelial cells squeeze out secretion.
  • Striated ducts (basal infoldings + mitochondria) modify saliva electrolytes.
  • Pleomorphic adenoma = commonest salivary tumour (parotid); Sjögren → dry mouth.
